draft.title: The photoelectric effect
card: When light shines on a metal surface, it can eject electrons from the metal. These electrons are called photoelectrons.
Ejection happens only if the light is above a threshold frequency, which depends on the metal. Below it, no electrons are ejected, however bright the light is.
Above the threshold frequency, even very dim light ejects electrons straight away. Brighter light ejects more electrons per second, and a higher frequency gives each electron more kinetic energy.

The wave model predicted that a bright enough light of any frequency would eventually eject electrons. Einstein explained the effect with photons: one photon gives all its energy to one electron, and it must carry enough energy to free it.
draft.remember: Frequency decides whether electrons are ejected. Brightness decides how many.

a.q: Red light shining on a metal ejects no electrons, however bright it is. What does this show?
opts: The red light is below the metal's threshold frequency
The red light is too bright to eject electrons
The metal needs a longer time to absorb the red light
The red light has too many photons to eject electrons
a.why: Each photon of red light has too little energy to free an electron, so none are ejected. Making the light brighter only adds more photons of the same low energy, so it cannot help.
a.clue: Think about the energy of one photon, not the number of photons.

b.q: Violet light ejects electrons from a zinc plate. The light is then made much dimmer, but its colour is unchanged. What happens?
opts: Electrons are still ejected, but fewer each second
Electrons stop being ejected until the light is brighter
Electrons are ejected, but each has less kinetic energy
Electrons are ejected only after a long delay
b.why: The frequency is unchanged, so each photon still has enough energy to free an electron. Dimmer light has fewer photons, so fewer electrons are ejected each second. Dimness does not cause a delay or lower the energy of each photon.
b.clue: The colour stays the same, so the energy of each photon stays the same.

a.best: The red light is below the metal's threshold frequency

b.best: Electrons are still ejected, but fewer each second

problems.detail: Visible violet light (about 400 nm, about 3.1 eV) does not eject electrons from zinc. Zinc's work function is about 4.3 eV, so its threshold is in the ultraviolet. The classic zinc-plate demonstration needs UV light. Change the light to ultraviolet, or change the metal to one with a low work function such as sodium or potassium.

'A higher frequency gives each electron more kinetic energy' is imprecise. Higher frequency raises the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons (K_max = hf − φ), as the HSC syllabus teaches. Individual electrons can leave with less energy than this.

check.summary: Question b's setup is physically false: visible violet light cannot eject electrons from zinc, which needs ultraviolet light, so change the light to UV or the metal to sodium. The card should also say that higher frequency raises the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
